why_how.text: Driving legally in Illinois requires a valid Illinois license, and the vehicle’s gross vehicle weight rating determines its license classification.
A basic Illinois license for driving a car is Class D.

A Class D holder may drive a rental vehicle weighing up to twenty-six thousand pounds within Illinois when carrying personal property belonging to the driver or an immediate family member for a nonbusiness purpose.
For that personal-property rental exception, the rental company must supply safety-course information that the driver is required to complete successfully.
Special licensing requirements apply to school buses, religious-organization buses, child-care vehicles, for-profit ride-sharing vehicles and vehicles used to transport senior citizens.
Illinois stopped issuing Temporary Visitor Driver’s Licenses on July first, two thousand twenty-four; someone previously eligible for one may apply for a standard license.
The general minimum age for an Illinois driver’s license is sixteen, subject to the handbook’s listed age-specific conditions.
An applicant aged sixteen or seventeen must finish state-approved driver education, log fifty hours of practice and pass all three examination components to receive a license.
When a parent or guardian cannot accompany a minor applicant, a legal guardian or responsible adult older than twenty-one must sign the minor’s consent affidavit.

title.text: Young applicant conditions and License exemptions

why_how.text: A first-time applicant aged eighteen through twenty who has never held a license or finished an approved high-school or commercial driver-education program must complete a six-hour course from a state-certified adult driver-education provider.
A driver younger than eighteen cannot drive a for-hire property-delivery vehicle or a vehicle requiring a commercial license.
Drivers younger than twenty-one cannot operate for-hire vehicles carrying more than ten passengers, commuter vans, religious or school buses, senior-citizen transport vehicles or child-care vehicles.
A new Illinois resident with a valid license from elsewhere must obtain the Illinois license within ninety days of moving or before the existing license expires, whichever happens sooner.
A visitor passing through Illinois may drive using a valid license issued by the visitor’s home state or country.
An out-of-state college or university student in Illinois, along with that student’s spouse and children, may drive on valid licenses from their home jurisdiction.
Active-duty members of the United States Armed Forces and the spouses and dependent children living with them may drive on valid home-state licenses.

An Illinois resident serving in the military outside the United States may use a previously obtained license deferral for the first one hundred twenty days after returning; the returning resident’s spouse and dependent children living with the resident share that provision.

The same one-hundred-twenty-day return provision, with a deferral obtained beforehand, covers Illinois-resident civilian employees of the Armed Forces or Defense Department serving abroad and their spouses and dependent children living with them.

Illinois keeps a record of a licensed driver’s traffic violations and crashes, including convictions received in other states. When a nonresident commits an Illinois violation requiring immediate action, Illinois creates a record and reports the violation to the person’s home state.
